entry.title: Starting small
entry.content:
Example post: Replace this sample with your own writing.

A first version does not need to answer every question. It needs to make the next question easier to ask.

Pick one useful thing

Before choosing tools, write down what someone should be able to do. A sentence like “find the note I saved last week” is a clearer starting point than a long feature list.

Make the loop short

Build enough to try the idea, use it, and notice what feels awkward. Short feedback loops make it easier to change direction while the work is still small.

Leave room to improve

Keep a short list of what you deliberately left out. That list helps distinguish a missing requirement from a feature that can wait.

The next step for this example: choose one real project and describe its smallest useful version.
entry.summary: An example note on giving an idea a manageable first version.

entry.title: Notes that help later
entry.content:
Example post: Replace this sample with your own writing.

A useful note helps your future self understand what mattered. Saving the source is only the beginning.

Capture the reason

Alongside a link or quote, add one sentence about why you saved it. That sentence is often the most useful part when you return weeks later.

Use a small structure

Try three prompts:

  • Idea: What is the point worth remembering?
  • Context: Where might it be useful?
  • Next step: Is there anything to try?

Revisit before reorganizing

A collection grows more useful when you use it. Read a few old notes before spending an afternoon inventing new categories.

Replace this sample with a real idea, a source you want to remember, and one concrete way you used it.
entry.summary: An example approach to capturing ideas with enough context.
